↳ Posted by JACKB on June 22nd, 2009.

Also known as Marbhna Luimni (which means the dead of Limerick) but more usually called in English Limerick’s Lamentation. It is a Jacobean tune lamenting the defeat of the Irish-Jacobean forces at the siege of Limerick in 1691. As a lament it is usually played very slowly and with feeling.

↳ Posted by David50 on October 17th, 2014.

Lochaber no More - the song

The words for the song Lochaber No More are in “The poems of Allan Ramsay, Volume 2” published in 1800 (Google Books has it). Some web sources say that it was first published in his “Tea-Table Miscellany” of 1724 but I don’t see it in the copy of that on archive.org.

The words, titled “Lochaber”, and tune (with a harmony part) are in Vol 2 of W. Thomson’s “Orpheus Caledonius” of 1733 - http://digital.nls.uk/special-collections-of-printed-music/pageturner.cfm?id=91481498&mode=transcription. It was in the 1755 edition - the link from a search at digital.nls.uk is too long to give.

Page 371 of James Hogg’s “The Forest Minstrel” of 1810 (Google books has it), referring to the song, links the tune to one called “Lord Ronald my son”.

marbhna luimnigh

the definitive version of marbhna luimnigh is the ceoltoiri chualann rendering in the gaiety concert dublin in 1969. sean potts is magnificent at the start of the piece on tin whistle and the air is played beautifully with perfect timing by the whole group. mind you, the reformed ceoltoiri chualann did a great job of it in 1972 at the tribute concert to o riada with paddy moloney on the pipes in charge.

Irish Lamentations, X:7

This setting, probably the best I’ve come across, appears as “Caoine Luimnighe ”in the Roche Collection, Vol 4, No. 65. For consistency with other postings, I have transposed from the Amix in which it appears there, and also removed the various slurs, grace notes etc. in order to improve readibility. Anyone seeking the original can find it at http://www.itma.ie/digitallibrary/scorch_file/roche_vol-4/10829/750. The ‘variation’ shown, which I presume is for a “last time only” ending, comes with the note “olagón”, which is Irish for “lament” (but with loud wailing rather than quiet sobs).

↳ Posted by Harald Wellmann on April 13th, 2020.

Lochaber No More, X:11

This setting is transcribed from the title track on the Boys of the Lough album, “Lochaber No More”. They describe it as a Slow March and on the recording play it quite slow and will often draw out notes at the end of phrases. I feel like Irish Lamentation is different enough from this setting that they could be considered different tunes but maybe I’m just not understanding the connection. Perhaps the BOTL setting is just real out there considering the lyrics for the song Lochaber No More are frequently sung to the tune of Irish Lamentation…..

Anyways, I really love this tune and will often play it in either Amix or Gmix. Both get a slightly different feel.

↳ Posted by DUHEM VERONIQUE on February 23rd, 2025.

Limerick Lamentation, X:13

I play version 9 on the pipes, and this setting on the clarsach (wire strung harp such as Brian Boru Harp or Queen Mary Harp).

This version 13 is a transposition from version 9 down to Dmaj with updates (for instance on Cs).

This tune was most probably composed on a clarsach and you cannot change the heights of a string while playing the tune. Either F# or F natural, either C# or C natural, not both # and natural.

And in Gmaj, the F are sharps.

Assumption have been made that in such a case the player may have sung the F natural instead of playing it. But it’s looks complex. Today’s versions potentially come from the song which have been sung base on the melody, song translated back to music in Gmaj.

The only way I find to play this tune on my clarsach is going down to Dmajor and playing C natural.

By doing so, I outscope the range of pipes / whistle / flute by going down the low A, and I loose the so nice alternates from F# to F natural because I cannot play both C# and C natural in the same rendition.

But it’s potentially closer to what may have been composed and played on a clarsach.

Limerick Lamentation, X:16 Lochaber No More : transcribed from Boys of the Lough

I’ve played this wonderful tune since I first heard it live in a concert around the time of the album by Boys of the Lough. (c1976) Many people have asked me about it’s time signature, which I hadn’t really worried about until I clicked on the title in “thesess” discography and discover a minefield of different versions. I’d love to know where BotL got their version, as it is significantly different to Limerick Lamentation or Marbha Luimni, which I have also played for years without noticing much similarity.
Looking at the notation for the tune I tried to capture it as a slow march, but eventually found it fitted a 3/2 structure. [I can’t post that here as it is listed as 3/4]
Some notes are held a moment longer for phrasing, notably in Bars 2 & 4. So the piece becomes a Slow Air/Lament.
Slow the tempo down right down.

here is the 3/2 version

C: transcribed from Boys of the Lough
D:Boys of The Lough
N: notation C Hamblin
R:slow march
Q:120
M:3/2
L:1/4
K:Edor
